The revival of Noel Coward's Private Lives that opened Thursday night at the Theatre is a welcome reminder of how sophisticated comedy used to sound when it was written by someone who knew what sophisticated meant.
The production succeeds in large part because of the casting of Kim Cattrall and Paul Gross.
Amanda and Elyot enjoy each other as much as they annoy each other, and the performers' playful rapport makes their guilty pleasure infectious.
For the most part, Coward's louche shenanigans feel remarkably modern.
Cattrall, an experienced stage actress, is easier to admire than adore as Amanda...until, that is, she starts to bellow like a shrew, which is all too often.
Yet Richard Eyre's production largely fails to land even the easy laughs.

I once saw a "Blithe Spirit" directed by Harold Pinter for London's National Theatre in which virtually every laugh was killed by Pinter's apparent desire to explore the dark underbelly of Noël Coward's frothy comedy. Director Richard Eyre hasn't gone quite that far with "Private Lives.

cn.t: This revival earns mixed-to-positive reviews, with critics praising Cattrall's star turn and the production's wit, but some fault director Eyre's naturalistic approach for dampening Coward's signature sparkle and sophistication.

vs.sum: The Music Box Theatre offers excellent sightlines from most seats, making it ideal for intimate dramas, though sound quality can vary. The theater's charming Georgian-inspired design adds to its ambiance, while comfort and facilities are average for a Broadway venue.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
